verdicts.evidence: The load-bearing step - interpolating $300m of 1920 direct mail back to '$200-250m' for 1914 - fails three independent cross-checks. (1) Share of total: $300m against Coen's 1920 total of $2,480m is 12.1 percent, against HSUS T 444's $2,935m it is 10.2 percent; applying either share to 1914 gives about $133m, not $200-250m. (2) Price level: the CPI roughly doubled 1914-1920, so $300m of 1920 direct mail is about $150m at 1914 prices for the same real volume, and real volume grew over the period, so the 1914 nominal figure must sit well under $150m on that route. (3) Upper bound from the next observed year: I read HSUS series T 464 off p. 857 and direct mail in 1935 was $282m against a T 444 total of $1,690m, i.e. 16.7 percent - a Depression-elevated share. The defensible 1914 band is therefore roughly 10-17 percent of total, or $120-190m, not $200-250m. Rebuilding the record's own components with that: 120-190 (direct mail) + 30-45 (mail-order keyed print) + 30-50 (patent medicine keyed press) + 40-70 (premiums, samples, novelties) = $220-355m, or 18.3-29.6 percent of $1,200m. Central lands near 24, not 32, and the superlative fails: at 24 percent direct response is statistically indistinguishable from local retail at 23 percent.

verdicts.evidence: I read HSUS series T 485-486 off p. 857 directly and it starts in 1928, not 1936 as the method's framing implies, so more evidence was available than the method used. Every anchor the method cites checks out (1936 265,475/1,380,121 = 19.24 percent; 1938 20.81; 1940 20.72). But the fuller series undercuts the argument used to push 1914 down. Classified's share of 52-city linage was 19.19 percent in 1928, 18.21 in 1929, 18.07 in 1930, 18.51 in 1933, 19.24 in 1936, 20.81 in 1938 - i.e. it sat in a tight 18-21 percent band while total linage collapsed 44 percent from 1929 to 1933. The stated ci80 upper bound of 18 sits below every single observation in the only series that exists (minimum 18.07). Under an honest interval test, the band must at least admit the possibility that 1914 was at the 1928-40 level.

verdicts.evidence: I attacked the tax arithmetic and it moves the answer up, not down. The Revenue Act of 1942 did replace the 35-60 percent graduated excess-profits schedule with a flat 90 percent rate - but it paired that with two features that both raise the after-tax cost of a deductible dollar, and the claim's method names one of them and then declines to act on it. (1) An overall ceiling limited combined normal tax, surtax and excess-profits tax to 80 percent of surtax net income. (2) A post-war refund credit of 10 percent of the excess-profits tax. The NBER's own marginal-tax-rate methodology computes the ceiling case explicitly as R = 0.8 x 0.9 = 0.72, i.e. a 72 percent effective marginal rate and a 28-cent after-tax cost per deductible dollar. The full grid of cases: 90 percent rate with the credit ignored = 10 cents; 90 percent with the credit valued = 19 cents; at the 80 percent ceiling with the credit ignored = 20 cents; at the ceiling with the credit valued = 28 cents. So the realistic range is 10-28 cents, the modal cases cluster at 19-20 cents, and the claim's ci80 top of 25 cents excludes the ceiling-plus-credit case that the standard methodology computes. The claim's own method concedes 'secondary accounts of the period settle on the government might pay up to 80 percent, implying about 20 cents' and then sets the central at 15 anyway - a downward pull with nothing behind it.

Most excess-profits payers sat at or near the ceiling, so the modal figure is 19-20 cents; central set at 20, interval spanning all four cases. Secondary accounts of the period ('the government might pay up to 80 percent') agree with the 20-cent figure.

open_defect.source_carries_the_error: The figure is NOT a paraphrase error introduced by this project: the R3 verdict on this claim quotes the cited Wikipedia article as saying the 21 ads 'amounted to nearly 20% of the 61 spots available', and R3 imported that string verbatim. verdicts.disagreement: Two interval-honesty concerns that do not change the verdict on the arithmetic. (1) The point CIs are a FLAT multiplicative band - implied wedge exactly [0.85, 0.98] - at every year from 1980 to 2007. So 1980, where the wedge is an exact identity with zero uncertainty, carries the same band as 2007, twenty-seven years out of sample. The band should collapse at 1980 and widen with distance from it. (2) The band captures only wedge uncertainty and carries no term for category drift, even though the restricted base's outdoor member changes from Billboards ($578m in 1980) to Out of Home ($7,202m in 2007), a definitional widening the dataset itself measures at 2.77x. gaps_not_bridged and the known_direction_of_error note are otherwise candid and correct.
